transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim - Redwood (AE); Devon Patel - Redwood (SE); Maya Reyes - ArborComms (CTO); Jonah Kim - ArborComms (Infra Lead); Priya Desai - ArborComms (Product)

Summary: quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming responses, burst concurrency profiles, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense given data residency + throughput needs. Agreed to run token/sec benchmarks and a follow-up technical session.

Topics: p95 SLOs, streaming chunking, concurrency (steady-state and burst), model variants and quantization tradeoffs, Dedicated capacity sizing, VPC/private deployment constraints, audit logs/KMS.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sara (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining we can do quick intros, we have about 45 minutes.
[00:05] Maya (ArborComms): Hi all, Maya here. We run a real-time call-transcription+summarization product embedded in our contact center platform. Latency is critical for us, p95 end-to-end ideally under 400ms for 256 token responses but we also have long summaries up to 2k tokens for post-call processing.
[00:20] Jonah (ArborComms): Jonah, infra lead. We're on AWS and using reserved instances today, using g4/g5 for microservices. Concerned about spikes during business hours — we see token surges.
[00:30] Devon (Redwood-SE): Thanks, quick note: when you say p95 under 400ms for 256 tokens, is that user-perceived time (streaming first-token latency) or complete generation time? Those are different SLOs.
[00:40] Priya (ArborComms): For the live UI the first token matters a lot. For the post-call long summaries it's ok if total generation takes longer up to a few seconds so long as throughput doesn't blow up our cost.
[01:05] Sara: Ok understood. Our typical pattern for customers with similar constraints is host the live stream via Redwood Hosted for lowest friction, and use Dedicated or Private for regulated or sustained high-throughput workloads. But we should dig into numbers — do you have current token/sec and concurrency metrics?
[01:22] Maya: We average 120 concurrent live sessions during peak, bursts up to 380 concurrent for 5-10 minutes. Each live session streams, average token output rate roughly 8 tokens/s per session while active. Post-call summary jobs are batched, currently around 600 parallel jobs at night, each producing ~1.5k tokens.
[01:40] Devon: Ok that helps. Quick math: 380 concurrent * 8 tok/s is ~3,040 tokens/s sustained during a burst. For p95 latency at user-visible streaming we look at first token + steady token throughput. With typical small models first-token p95 can be under 150-250ms on optimized GPUs; long-output token/sec depends on batching, KV cache hits, and whether you stream token-by-token or chunk.
[02:12] Jonah: Right, and our requirement is first-token p95 <= 350ms for live. For the post-call batch jobs we want cost predictability — could be Dedicated with pre-warmed pools. Also we have strict data residency rules and need KMS for keys.
[02:30] Devon: For KMS and audit logs, our Private deployment (VPC/private control plane) supports BYOK and HSM integrations; Dedicated also supports customer-managed keys depending on contract. We can share our security checklist.
[02:45] Maya: Is there a big perf diff between Hosted and Dedicated? We assume Dedicated could give more predictable p95 but are worried about cost.
[02:55] Sara: Good question. Hosted is great for fast time-to-value and can hit low latencies for moderate load. Dedicated gets you predictable throughput and tail latencies because you control the GPU pool and autoscale policy. Cost per-token is often lower at scale on Dedicated but requires commitment. For spikes we have burst pools and routing fallbacks to cheaper models or cross-region routing — but that can affect latency.
[03:23] Priya: How do you manage fallback without hurting user experience? If we route to a smaller model during a spike we may see quality regressions.
[03:33] Devon: We use policy-based routing: for latency-critical routes we prefer dedicated high-tier nodes with aggressive autoscale. Fallbacks kick in only when all capacity tiers are exhausted; they can route to a quantized or shorter-context model and return a confidence flag. Also we can replicate an A/B evaluation set to validate fallback quality.
[03:55] Jonah: About 350ms p95 for first token — is that realistic for a streaming multi-turn convo in Hosted?
[04:05] Devon: For Hosted, if you need strict 350ms p95 consistently at ~3k tok/s sustained bursts, it's borderline — depends on model size and sequence length. Hosted sharing of resources can sometimes increase tail if other tenants spike. Dedicated gives much more headroom. If you pick a small-chat-optimized model and tune batching, we can get under 350ms for first token.
[04:35] Maya: What about long summaries 1.5k tokens — how do you size Dedicated pools for that?
[04:42] Devon: For large off-line batches we recommend separate capacity class — larger batch workers with high throughput configuration. We size by token/sec and concurrency for those jobs. For example, one p4d-style machine can process X tokens/s for model Y — we'll run a baseline to determine exact numbers. The typical approach is: host streaming pool + offline batch pool and schedule night batching to avoid spikes.
[05:05] Sara: We should schedule a benchmark run: you provide sample prompts and we run token/sec and p95 latency tests across Hosted and Dedicated small cluster configurations. Devon will prepare the harness.
[05:18] Priya: Also, network egress and VPC configuration — our legal needs IP whitelisting and audit logs.
[05:25] Devon: Noted. For Private we can deploy a control plane inside your VPC and integrate with your SAML SSO, RBAC mapping, and KMS; we can also ship logs to your SIEM. For Dedicated we provide audit logs and can integrate to your KMS, but Private gives you the most network isolation.
[06:00] Maya: Are there any gotchas with prefix/KV cache when streaming? We sometimes reuse conversation context and want cache hits to reduce tokens and latency.
[06:12] Devon: Yes, prefix/KV caching is critical. If you have long-running sessions with repeated prompts, KV cache reduces compute on subsequent tokens but you still pay for tokens. Caching heuristics depend on conversation fragmentation. We'll look at your prompt distribution to set cache TTLs.
[06:30] Jonah: For benchmarking, we'd like to see p95 numbers for both first-token and full-generation for three model sizes: small (chat-small), medium (chat-medium quantized), large (chat-large server). Also measure token/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
[06:45] Devon: That's a good matrix. We'll test the models on Hosted (to show baseline), then run Dedicated with 1 and 3-node pools and measure p95 and median latencies under steady and burst loads. We'll produce CSV/Google Sheet results and a summary doc.
[07:02] Priya: Out of curiosity, competitors like DeepServe claim <200ms p95 consistently — are those realistic?
[07:10] Sara: Competitors often run smaller models or very aggressive batching with low context length, which helps. It's doable for certain workloads, but for mixed live streaming + long summaries, there's often tradeoffs. We'll show the tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[07:30] Maya: What about autoscaling behavior? During a 10-minute spike to 380 concurrent sessions we need consistent response, scaling shouldn't be too slow.
[07:40] Devon: Autoscale reaction times depend on the policy. Dedicated pre-warmed pools and predictive autoscaling (based on traffic patterns) work best. For Hosted we have warm-burst options but less control. We'll document scaling windows and recommend pre-warm thresholds for your traffic patterns.
[08:10] Jonah: Also we need to understand warmup/KV cache cold-starts for long conversations — cold starts inflate p95.
[08:20] Devon: Right. For steady-state long-running sessions we ensure sticky routing to maintain cache locality. Also we can provision a small set of long-lived workers to keep KV in memory for hot sessions.
[08:36] Maya: Pricing is a big decision factor. If Dedicated reduces unit cost by 30% but requires a 6‑12 month commit, we have to weigh operational risk.
[08:48] Sara: We'll include a per-token cost comparison and a sample committed plan. We can also propose a pilot: start Hosted for an initial period while we run benchmarks and then move to Dedicated with a short-term commit if numbers justify it.
[09:10] Priya: For legal, can you share SOC 2 + data flow diagrams?
[09:16] Sara: Yes will attach SOC 2 report and the private deployment checklist.
[09:22] Devon: One more technical question: do you encrypt at rest per customer and want single-tenant GPUs?
[09:30] Maya: We need per-customer KMS-backed encryption for persisted artifacts and logs, not necessarily single-tenant GPUs but prefer dedicated pools for isolation.
[09:40] Devon: That works — Dedicated + customer-managed keys is a common pattern. For Private it's BYOK by default.
[10:05] Sara: Ok quick recap — action items: Devon will build benchmark harness and test three models; Sara will send pricing and security docs; Maya will send sample prompt sets and SLOs. We'll aim to run benchmarks next week and have a 60-min technical run with your infra team.
[10:25] Maya: Sounds good. One last thing — can you include an evaluation of streaming chunk size vs token/sec? We sometimes see smaller chunks increase overhead.
[10:34] Devon: Yes we'll include chunk-size experiments (1 token vs 8 token chunks) and measure p95 and effective cost.
[10:45] Jonah: Great. Thanks everyone.
[10:50] Sara: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and materials.
